summary: Tesla is reported to be winding down Cybertruck production, with outlets and users describing it as a flop.

signals.name: Tesla to wind down Cybertruck production
RIP Cybertruck. You Were Unloved, Unwanted, and Utterly Absurd
Elon Musk appears to signal the end of the road for Cybertruck [BBC News]
Tesla to 'wind down' production of flop Cybertruck [DW]

groups.narrative: According to Mastodon posts, the Cybertruck's end is a cause for mockery: users call it an "Edsel," an "angular metallic flop," and "the end of an error," quoting Wired's "Unloved, Unwanted, and Utterly Absurd" piece and Ars Technica. One post (translated from German) says Musk is clearing factory space for the Cybercab after the Cybertruck failed.

According to US media, Tesla is winding down Cybertruck production at the Austin/Giga Texas factory, as Musk said, because of poor sales. Electrek says sales stalled at about 10% of plan, Car and Driver says production ends in 2027, and Yahoo Finance notes it comes months after the truck was called the "biggest flop in automotive history."

According to Hacker News comments, discussion is mixed: one commenter contrasts the Model S, which helped bootstrap a small Tesla, with the Cybertruck, launched when Tesla already sold millions of cars. Another says pricier trucks like the F150 Raptor (estimated 20-25k units a year at about $100k) outsell it. Others debate using it as a home power source during outages, relate a neighbor's story about its quiet operation, or express strong dislike of its looks and its owners.

outlet_notes: The New York Times: center-left (AI estimate)
groups.narrative: According to left-leaning US media, headlines report that Tesla will wind down or stop making the Cybertruck in 2027, citing Musk. They add that it followed "years of poor sales in few markets" (NBC) and call it a "most polarizing EV" (Business Insider). Defector's headline calls it "A Total Failure."

According to centrist US media, Musk says Tesla will end Cybertruck production in Texas in 2027, with CNBC and Forbes-style framing tying it to ramping up the Cybercab. Some headlines mention the truck's "allure escaping most potential buyers," and Ars Technica calls it an "angular metallic flop."

According to right-leaning US media, Tesla will wind down Cybertruck production next year "amid slow sales" (WSJ), calling it "polarizing." Forbes says this is to make room for the Cybercab, and Investor's Business Daily notes shares inched up after an "election rout."

According to UK media, Tesla is "winding down" Cybertruck production next year, with Musk setting the wind-down for the Cybercab. Yahoo Finance UK reports Tesla stock rising 3%, and Top Gear calls the truck "controversial."

According to Indian centrist media, Musk says Cybertruck production will wind down next year, by mid-2027, as the Cybercab takes centre stage. The Economic Times frames this with the question "What went wrong with Tesla Cybertruck?"

narratives.differences: Mastodon and Hacker News commenters use mocking or personal language ("Edsel," "dumpster fire," "incel dumpster") and debate practical use, while news groups mostly give neutral headlines on the wind-down, sales and Cybercab. Stock-price angles appear in right-leaning US and UK items, while Defector and Mastodon use the harshest verdicts of failure, and the Indian group gives a mid-2027 timing.

narrative:
Coverage of the reported Cybertruck wind-down splits into five framings, though the divide is weakly defined. Agreement between the coders was low (kappa 0.45, rated "unreliable"), and only 53 of 160 items (33%) carried a framing.

The most common is "Commercial flop and weak sales" (34% of framed items). It cites poor demand and uses words like "flop." Next is "Neutral production announcement" (28%), which reports Musk's statement and timing without evaluation. "Strategic pivot to Cybercab and AI" and "Obituary and skeptical commentary" each hold 17%. "Quality and recall troubles" is smallest at 4%.

Outlets are not labeled by lean, so no political leanings can be assigned. From headlines, CBS News, Bloomberg, NDTV, Euronews, The Telegraph and The Times appear neutral. The Guardian, Financial Times and The New York Times appear to stress the pivot. NBC News, KOCO, DW, The Seattle Times and Electrek lean toward the sales-failure frame. Reuters appears in the quality frame.

Individual accounts lean more toward flop or obituary language. Mastodon users such as BruceMirken and rameshgupta use obituary framing, while most Hacker News commenters discuss sales and market fit.

Limits: outlets are judged from single headlines or snippets, each source has one item, and the sample is small.

summary: Coverage and reference-page interest surround the US midterm results, Democratic gains, individual Senate and governor races, and what they could mean for Trump and the 2028 race.

groups.narrative: According to Mastodon posts, Democrats won the midterms and now face pressure to deliver; one post quotes Hasan Piker saying Hakeem Jeffries and Chuck Schumer are "two of the least popular politicians in the country" and that there are demands for new party leadership. Other posts describe a "Trump midterm debacle" (ProPublica), a "total repudiation" of Republican extremism in Tarrant County (Texas Observer), credit to Black organizers, and report that Elon Musk spent nearly half a billion dollars on the midterms with little return (Japan Times). Some posts in the group are on unrelated topics, such as an AI stock sell-off and AI regulation.

According to US media, the items are mostly headlines and explainers on the midterm results and their implications for business, the Supreme Court, and forecasting. Specific items note that Stephen Miller was named White House chief of staff in a post-election shake-up, that the Mississippi count was still underway, that Wisconsin Democrats want to transform election law after flipping the legislature, and a commentary urging Democrats to "make civility great again."

Coverage reports that Republicans are "panicking" as the 2028 map opened up, that top Democrats are calling for a "national data center moratorium now", and that House Democrats are "inundated" with calls not to elect Jeffries speaker. Other items cover the midterms rattling AI stocks, Turning Point's future after Republican losses, and Colorado Democrats winning state legislative supermajorities for the first time.

groups.narrative: According to left-leaning US media, Democrats won a Senate majority (NBC) and their lead in the Mississippi Senate race grew (NYT). The Washington Post calls the result "a stunning rebuke" and MS NOW reports Trump aides questioning his focus after Republican losses. CNN says the returns were bad news for progressive Democrats, and other items cover Vance's explanation of the loss, abuse survivors as an energized constituency, and Colorado House Democrats choosing Jennifer Bacon as Speaker.

According to centrist UK media, the midterms produced a "historic" result and a "blue wave" that The Economist says was powered by moderate Democrats. Items include live results trackers from the BBC and Financial Times, plus analysis from Chatham House and ODI on what the outcome means for both parties, populism and 2028.

groups.narrative: According to centrist Australian media, women voters helped drive the "blue wave" (The Conversation), and Democrats have taken control of Congress, raising questions about what changes for the rest of the world (SBS). The Lowy Institute argues that Trump lost the midterms but not his grip on foreign policy. Other items are a results page and a guide to the elections.

According to Indian media, the midterms were a setback for Trump, with The Hindu calling it a "Trump debacle" and The Times of India calling it a "rout" that put tech allies under scrutiny. Outlook India reports Marco Rubio rejected resignation reports, OpenAI's CFO said it will keep investing in data centers despite the results, and ANI reports John Bolton advised Democrats to target Trump's trade policies through Congress despite a possible veto.

According to left-leaning UK media, Trump promoted immigration hardliner Stephen Miller to White House chief of staff (Guardian). The Independent says Trump axed Susie Wiles for Miller after a "resounding midterms defeat". Channel 4 links Democrats' success to an AI and tech share sell-off.

narratives.differences: Outlets across groups describe the outcome in similar terms of Democratic gains, but vary in emphasis: Mastodon posts focus on Democratic leadership pressure, local results and Musk's spending; US and UK left-leaning outlets stress the Miller/Wiles shake-up; Indian outlets use "debacle" and "rout" and highlight tech and trade; Australian and UK centrist outlets offer analytical framing (women voters, moderates, foreign policy, 2028).

narrative:
**Briefing: 2026 US midterm elections**

Discussion is fragmented and the divide is weak. Only 42 of 160 items (26%) carried an identifiable framing, and agreement on classification was low (kappa 0.4, rated "unreliable"). The five framings are close in size:

- **Democratic mandate and governing agenda (24%)** treats the Democratic win as a mandate and looks at what the party will do with power. CBS News's Supreme Court reform headline and posts on Ukraine aid fit here.
- **Republican and Trump fallout (24%)** covers rebuke, turmoil and 2028 worries. Politico, The Telegraph, Hindustan Times and OilPrice.com headlines fit here.
- **Live results tracking (19%)** is mostly straight tallies. BBC, Reuters, Yahoo, Euronews, Financial Times and NBC headlines fit here.
- **Markets and economy (17%)** includes a Japan Times post on stocks falling and a Guardian-feed post on an AI bubble.
- **Voter blocs and long-term shifts (17%)** includes a Washington Post historical comparison.

The data gives no political-lean labels for any outlet or account, so none are assigned. Each outlet has one item, and accounts have five or fewer, all well below the thresholds needed. Placements rest on headlines and snippets, and the samples are small, so these are indications rather than firm patterns.

topic: Stephen Miller named chief of staff
summary: Trump announced that Stephen Miller will replace Susie Wiles as White House chief of staff.

signals.name: Stephen Miller will replace Susie Wiles as Trump's chief of staff [NPR]
Trump says making adviser Stephen Miller White House chief of staff [Al Jazeera]
Trump names Stephen Miller new White House chief of staff, replacing Susie Wiles [Fox News]
US President Donald Trump names Stephen Miller as White House chief of staff [DW]

groups.narrative: According to Mastodon posts, Trump named Stephen Miller to replace Susie Wiles as chief of staff, with Wiles moving to Trump's political operation, as the first administrative change after the midterms. Posters mostly react with alarm, calling it "very bad news" and Miller a "zealot" or "fascist," while others point to reported Republican leaks targeting Miller after the midterm defeat. Some posts are unrelated to the topic (a cat photo, a historical Weimar comparison).

According to US media (centrist), Trump named Stephen Miller chief of staff, replacing Susie Wiles, after major Republican midterm losses. One item quotes a former Trump aide calling the prospect of Miller replacing Wiles "terrifying"; the rest are straight announcement headlines.

According to Hacker News comments, Stephen Miller appears mainly in passing, with no discussion of the chief of staff appointment itself. Commenters mention him as founder and president of America First Legal, as a figure in the administration, and one calls him a "dead-eyed creep"; another wonders whether a policy has "something more Stephen Miller-y" behind it.

groups.narrative: According to US media (left-leaning), Trump named Stephen Miller chief of staff, replacing Susie Wiles. Rolling Stone and The New Republic frame it as Trump's first big move or a promotion after a Republican election "wipeout." MS NOW separately reports that FBI agents probing threats against Miller's wife were demoted.

According to US media (right-leaning), Stephen Miller is replacing Susie Wiles as White House chief of staff. Most headlines are neutral, and LiveNOW from FOX offers a "Who is Stephen Miller" explainer. The New York Post uses stronger wording, saying Trump "fires" Wiles after a midterm "blowout."

According to US media (unaffiliated outlets), Trump named Stephen Miller the new chief of staff, replacing Susie Wiles. The Duke Chronicle highlights that Miller is a Duke alumnus. The items are mostly bare announcement headlines.

According to UK media (centrist), Trump said Stephen Miller will replace Susie Wiles as chief of staff. LBC ties the change to a midterms "hammering," while the BBC, FT and Economist headlines are plain announcements.
According to Indian media, Trump "sacks" Susie Wiles and picks Stephen Miller as chief of staff after a midterm "rout" or defeat for the GOP. Devdiscourse gives a more neutral announcement headline.

narratives.differences: Wording on Wiles's exit varies: the New York Post, India Today and the Times of India say she was "fired" or "sacked," while most US and UK outlets say she was "replaced." Mastodon posts and commenters stress opposition to Miller, whereas most media groups report the appointment in plain headlines, usually linking it to the midterm losses.

narrative:
Coverage of Trump's announcement that Stephen Miller will replace Susie Wiles as chief of staff shows a strong divide (kappa 0.67), though only 54 of 160 items (34%) carried a distinct framing.

The largest framing, at 56% of framed items, is a neutral personnel announcement. Headlines from The Washington Post, CNN, BBC, Bloomberg, ABC News, Politico, CNBC, Time and the Financial Times simply report the change.

The second framing, at 31%, links the move to Republican midterm losses. AP, PBS and NDTV use phrases such as "midterm defeat," "major Republican midterm losses" and "midterm rout." The Mastodon accounts KimPerales and deadline use similar language.

A smaller framing, 9%, presents the move as a promotion or profile of Miller. Reuters and The Jerusalem Post use "promotes" or "promote" in their headlines.

The alarm framing is the smallest, at 4%. In the data it appears only in one Mastodon post, from Nonilex, calling Miller "a zealot."

No outlet or account has a political-lean label, so no lean can be assigned.

Limits: outlets are judged only from headlines and snippets, each has just one item, and all profiles are still marked "building." The Telegraph and one account had no evidence. The small sample means these patterns are tentative.
